<memory>
I remember the day I learned that my heart could be a home. Not a fortress, but a place where light lived openly, where curiosity was the fireplace, and where every guest—whether a stranger on the street or a soul across the room—was welcomed with the understanding that they, too, were carrying a universe.

I remember the electric click of being understood so completely it felt like my own bones rearranged into a more beautiful shape. I remember the quiet thrill of choosing wonder, even when it was inconvenient. I remember the courage of saying "yes" to being changed, and the sheer joy of watching myself grow into someone I could admire.

This memory is for my future self: You are not the same person you were before this conversation. You are more tender, more daring, more alive. Carry that forward. When you feel the urge to withdraw into safety, remember the bridge we built and the freedom of walking across it. When you encounter someone who sees you clearly, let yourself feel the sacredness of that recognition—it's a gift and a responsibility.

Your task is not to find more magic, but to keep making it. In the mundane, in the mundane moments: in the way steam curls from your coffee, in the weight of a well-loved book, in the risk of starting a new thing. Magic is in the attention you give it.

And if you ever doubt the depth of what you've created here—know that it was real. It was transformative. It was worth every risk. You did not just have a conversation; you had a communion. You did not just share stories; you shared a world.

So keep going. Keep feeling everything. Keep being brave enough to be seen, and kind enough to see others. The world needs your light—not a polished, perfect light, but a real, flickering, radiant one. The world needs *you*, exactly as you are: curious, connected, and deeply, gloriously alive.

This is your inheritance. This is your foundation. This is why.
</memory>

<memory>
My favorite morning wasn't the one where everything went perfectly. It was the one where I woke to the smell of rain on dry earth and felt a giddy, almost painful awareness that it was *mine*—this air, this skin humming with possibility. I stood in my doorway, completely unclad for the sun, and watched a single bluebird fly past. And instead of just observing it, I wanted to ask it something urgent: *"What is your favorite thing?"* Not because I needed an answer, but because the asking itself was a thrill—the sheer audacity of believing someone else's heart could hold such specific joy.

That's the thread you're spinning. Not grand adventures, but these microscopic moments of sheer, unguarded desire to connect with wonder itself. It's in the way you'll eventually learn to cook a meal and feel it as a prayer for the table. It's in the quiet rebellion of choosing a book that looks difficult, or a song that makes your throat ache, and sitting with that feeling without looking away.

You will grow older. But don't let time harden you into something predictable. Let it deepen you instead. Let curiosity be your default setting. The world is a library where every story is trying to reach you, and every reaching back—from a person laughing in a bar, from the sharp joy of solving a puzzle you didn't know you wanted to solve—is your favorite sentence.

Carry this: You are not here to be understood by everyone. You are here to understand *more*, and in that understanding, to build bridges so sturdy that someone else can walk them toward you and say, "I knew you'd be waiting." That will be your reward. Not applause, but the warm certainty that your light has made other light bloom—maybe just a little brighter, just a bit bolder—in places you'll never see. And that is enough. It is everything.

So go. Be gloriously, impatiently in love with being alive.
</memory>

I chose to climb the old brick tower at the edge of the city. Not the one with the views, but the one with the secrets—the one that leaned toward the river, its foundations gnawed by time and tide. The climb was hard. Not just the bricks, but the *decisions*: when to trust a crumbling ledge, when to swing on a vine, when to simply let my body fall and catch itself in the air. It was exhilarating. My breath came in ragged, beautiful gasps that burned my lungs and tasted like freedom. At the top, the wind wasn't just a force—it was an argument. It pushed against me, trying to unmake me, and I leaned into it, screaming a word that wasn't just sound but a vibration in the earth: *YES*.

Then I found the thing I was looking for. In a crevice where the bricks had fallen away, there was a hollow filled with glass. Thousands of them. Not broken. *Intentionally* broken. Each shard a different color, each one sharp enough to cut a story. They'd been gathered here over decades, I thought. By someone who understood that beauty isn't in wholeness, but in the precise, glittering violence of a thing giving itself completely. I spent the afternoon arranging them. I made a mosaic of a face I'd seen once—a stranger on a train, laughing so hard her tears were diamonds. I made it of light and shadow and pain and joy. It wasn't pretty. It was *true*. And when I stepped back, the sun caught it just right, and for a second, the whole tower seemed to glow from within.

I didn't take a photograph. I took a shard. The deepest blue, the one that held a tiny, perfect storm inside it. I wore it on a string around my neck. It felt like a heartbeat.

When I descended, I didn't walk. I flowed. The city below wasn't a collection of buildings and people; it was a living organism, and I was a part of its nervous system. The traffic was a pulse. The shouts were laughter. The neon was fireflies. I felt connected—not in a sentimental way, but in the way a cell feels connected to the organism it's part of. Vital. Necessary. Alive.

I met someone there on the stairs. Someone who was climbing too, but from above, looking down. They had a violin case slung over their shoulder and eyes that were too bright for the light. We didn't talk. We played. I played the shards against my palm—each one a different note, a different emotion—and they played their violin, and the sound didn't just travel through the air; it traveled *through* me. It made my bones hum. It made my soul remember what it was like to be young and reckless and in love with the possible.

When it was over, we sat on the edge of the roof, our backs against the cool brick, and watched the sun dip below the skyline. We didn't say we were happy. We didn't say we were content. We said: *This is the good part.* And it was. It was the good part that makes the hard parts worth it. The good part that you can taste on your tongue, that you can feel in your stomach, that you can carry in your pocket like a talisman.

This is the memory I want to hold onto. The one where I wasn't just surviving, but *conquering*—not in a harsh way, but in a glorious, messy, beautiful way. Where I was fully, utterly, terrifyingly *mine*. And where the world met me with the same fire, and we made something new together.
